items.title: Protein quality control helps regulate circadian rhythms, study suggests
items.text: The body's internal circadian clock helps us feel sleepy at night and wake up in the morning. Using fruit flies, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have discovered that a cellular quality control process that removes defective proteins during protein synthesis helps regulate the pace of the circadian clock.

items.title: PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression
items.text: A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine. The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.

items.title: Mouse study reveals early eye damage in rare childhood disease
items.text: A study in mice that involved University of Manchester scientists has revealed that eye damage linked to a rare inherited childhood disease may begin remarkably early and worsen progressively over time. The team investigated deficiency in an enzyme called HGSNAT, the root cause of a devastating genetic childhood neurological disease called MPSIIIC, which produces progressive damage to the brain but can also affect vision. The findings are published in Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science.
